# Barrow Builders · Book II, pp. 34–47
# Generated by the extractor — fix the extractor, not this file.
PAGE	34
P	When the servants of the <b>Stone Lords</b> (page 382) rebelled, slaying their masters and unleashing the <b>Things Below</b> (page 412), those who died in the uprising were hailed as martyrs. The survivors raised mounds of earth and stone to honor them, simple barrows built with human hands and human arts.
P	Society collapsed. Horror swept the land.
P	Petty tyrants and sorcerer-kings rose to power. They had barrows built to honor loyal vassals or to seal away the ghosts of those they had betrayed.
P	Fleeting kingdoms rose and fell. Rulers raised grand barrows and had themselves interred with riches, slaves, and followers in tow. Fueled by dark magic and the power of the Things Below, some of these tyrants reigned on even after death.
P	In time, the power of the Things Below diminished. Subjects rose up and overthrew their masters. Tyrants began to fall.
P	Those who could not be killed were sealed away in barrows. The <b>current age</b> (page 414) arrived.
P	Many barrows still remain. A few are simple graves. Many are haunted or cursed.
P	Some imprison ancient evil. They dot the World's End, especially in the <b>Steplands</b> (page 372). The <b>Hillfolk</b> (page 228) shun them, and warn all travelers away. For they descended from the Barrow Builders, and those who cast them off. They know what horrors those earthen mounds contain.
H2	Names
HR
P	Breton- or Cornish-inspired, similar to <b>Hillfolk names</b> (page 228) but with more vowels: Alana, Arzhel, Brandan, Corent, Deniel, Enora, Gwenael, Herve, Judikael, Karenza, Katell, Maben, Margh, Nolwenn, Piran, Ronan, Winoc, Yanick, Yezekael.
H2	Hooks
HR
B	An artifact that the PCs want lies in a haunted barrow mound
B	Some fool unseals a barrow and lets <b>phantom riders</b> (page 45) loose
B	Someone acquires the tether of a <b>deathless one</b> (page 46)
B	Hillfolk are furious that one of the barrows was looted

H2	Themes
HR
P	Pick 1 or 2, or roll 1d12.
P	1d12 theme
HR
P	1 Revolution: hunting down the Stone Lords, upending the status quo
P	2 The works of the Makers: torn down, vandalized, repurposed, lost
P	3 Societal collapse: famine, shortage, hoarding, violence
P	4 Sorcerers and necromancers:
P	recklessly wielding power they can't control
P	5 Human sacrifice, blood magic, the courting and open worship of the Things Below
P	6 The horrors of war: pillaging, looting, slaughter, dislocation
P	7 Refugees, desperate and afraid, seeking safety, settling for survival
P	8 Sorcerer-kings and petty warlords with their grand, bloody ambitions
P	9 Conquest/oppression/enslavement
P	10 Intrigue/betrayal/civil war
P	11 Rulers clinging to power, even from the grave
P	12 Heroism and hope and perseverance, the casting off of tyrants, the slaying of monsters; the forging of a new age
H2	Questions
Q	Where is the nearest barrow-mound that you know of?
Q	What strange sign marks it?
Q	What tall tale have you heard of it?
Q	What story do you recall, from the terrible days after the Makers fell?
H2	Lore
HR
P	<b>Everyone knows:</b>
B	That old barrows dot the region
B	That they're smaller and cruder than Maker-ruins
B	That Hillfolk shun them
B	That they supposedly contain great treasure and great danger
P	<b>One might know:</b>
B	Where a few barrows can be found
B	That they were built by the Hillfolk's (reviled) ancestors
B	Of a particularly (in)famous figure among them
B	The horrors from those times
B	A tale about a specific barrow
P	<b>Very few know:</b>
B	What a given barrow contains
B	Where a specific figure is buried
B	The true story behind a barrow

H2	Sites
HR
P	Barrow Builder sites are most common in the <b>Steplands</b> (page 372), especially around <b>Blackwater Lake</b> (page 48) and <b>Three Coven Lake</b> (page 438). Plenty can also be found in the <b>Flats</b> (page 126), the <b>South Manmarch</b> (page 350), and along the <b>Dread River</b> (page 86). A few can be found in the <b>Huffel Peaks</b> (page 236) and as far north as the <b>Foothills</b> (page 144).
P	To create a Barrow Builder site, pick one or have someone roll the Die of Fate.
P	1d6 site
HR
P	1 A <b>cave</b> (page 380), in which they or their victims lived/hid/died/ were interred (combine with 1 or 2 themes, page 35)
P	2 An old battlefield or mass grave, likely <b>haunted</b> (page 72)
P	3-4 A <b>reclaimed Maker-ruin</b> (see below)
P	5-6 A <b>barrow</b> (page 39)

Maybe this was a plantation, with a small army of</i> <b><i>lithic servants</i></b> <i>For the Barrow Builders' theme, I roll an 11 ("rulers clinging to power, even from the</i> <i>grave"). For signs, I roll a 5 ("damage/plunder/vandalism/graffiti") and 10 ("crude,</i> <i>human-sized" modifications). For the current condition, I roll a 9 ("buried, overgrown…</i> <i>mostly intact"). I ponder a bit, and come up with this:</i> <i>A sorcerer led the humans here to rise up against their overseers. The sorcerer then claimed</i> <i>the manor as his own, along with the device that charged and controlled the lithic servants</i> <i>—a device powered by the Mindgem's makerglass heart! He turned the manor into a crude</i> <i>palace and sent "his" people back to work the fields. When they eventually rebelled, he was</i> <i>mortally wounded but transferred his soul into the device that ran the lithic servants.</i> <i>With his mind now spread among the many constructs, he squashed the uprising. His rule</i> <i>grew increasingly erratic, brutal, and ineffective. The tenements became more squalid and</i> <i>desperate. Folks fled. The sorcerer didn't care.</i>

H3	An old bronze dagger
P	<i>hand</i>, <i>magical</i>
P	Tinged green, but sharp and sturdy. In the chaotic days after the Makers fell, it was the weapon of a desperate father. He killed his own brother with it, to protect his children's food. He killed others, too, to make sure his family had enough. So many, many others.
P	The dagger holds a shard of that father's desperate will. When you <b><i>Seek Insight</i></b> <b><i>about someone while carrying the dagger</i></b>, add the following to the list of questions you can ask. If <b><i>your hand is on the hilt</i></b>, you can ask one of these questions for free, even on a 6-.
Q	What of mine do they most want?
Q	How am I most vulnerable to them?
Q	What do they carry that is useful to me?
P	If a PC keeps the dagger, treat it as a threat (a <i>MacGuffin</i>; <b>Instinct</b> to cause paranoia).

H3	The Three-star Crown
P	◇ <i>magical</i>, <i>beautiful</i>, Value 4
P	A circlet of whitest gold, set with three black sapphires that shine like stars. It was made by a renowned smith, an apprentice of the <b>Forge Lords</b> (page 156), at the command of a petty warlord. The warlord was so pleased, he maimed the smith's hands so that she could never make its rival. The smith killed herself in despair, cursing the crown to steal the hopes of all who wore it.
P	When you <b><i>wear the crown and interact</i></b> <b><i>with someone who fears or respects you</i></b>, you roll +CHA with advantage. Alas, <b><i>each time</i></b> <b><i>you don the crown</i></b>, roll +WIS: <b>on a 10+</b>, tell the GM one of your hopes and why you doubt it can be achieved; <b>on a 7-9</b>, tell them a hope you have abandoned; <b>on a 6-</b>, you fall into a deep despair that lasts until you rouse yourself to face a mortal danger.
P	If <b><i>the crown is destroyed</i></b>—the gems shattered, the metal reduced to slag—then the despair is lifted and all lost hopes are restored.
ICON	icons/treasure.svg
H3	A lead bracelet
P	<i>magical</i>, Value 1
P	This heavy, black metal torc is set with a red gem. It feels good upon your wrist.
P	Makes you feel important.
P	When you <b><i>wear the torc and threaten</i></b> <b><i>someone that you consider beneath you</i></b>, lose HP equal to the torc's current Cost (1d4 to start). They are filled with fear; the craven will flee, cower, or grovel, and even the brave will flinch and hesitate. Each time you use the torc, the Cost increases by 1 die size (max 1d10).
P	When you <b><i>wear the torc for a week without</i></b> <b><i>anyone questioning your authority</i></b>, decrease the Cost by one step (min 1d4).

H3	Banefire
P	Curtains or pillars of heatless flame, blue or green or purple, with no obvious source of fuel. Banefire features in many tales of the barrows: to repel, to imprison, or just as an uncanny feature of the mounds.
P	• Spring forth with little/no warning
P	• Blind them with sudden light
P	• Block a path or a line of sight
P	• Burn spirits, the undead, and living souls (d8 damage, ignores armor)
P	<b>Something interesting:</b> Ghosts and other spirits fear banefire as much as mortals, but the inhabitants of some barrows can control it.
P	<b>Something useful:</b> Banefire burns only where it's meant to; it never spreads. Each banefire is anchored to a blackened bone, all that remains of the mortal whose body and soul were sacrificed to fuel the flames.
HR
ICON	icons/danger.svg
H3	Traps
P	They put all that effort into building barrows. They weren't going to leave them unguarded.
P	To create a trap, consider the barrow's purpose and what it contains, and where the trap is found. Then pick or roll for the trap's intent, its trigger, its tell, and as many elements as makes sense. Imagine how it works. If you like, prep GM moves and/or an impending doom for the trap, and maybe a custom player move.
P	1d12 intent
HR
P	1-2 To kill/maim/injure
P	3-4 To repel/separate/deny/isolate
P	5-6 To weaken/hinder/delay
P	7-8 To capture/punish/torment
P	9-10 To alert/awaken/prepare
P	11-12 Roll d10 twice
P	1d12 trigger
HR
P	1-2 Stepping/entering/being/staying somewhere
P	3-4 Touching something
P	5-6 Moving something/picking it up
P	7-8 Breaking/disturbing something
P	9-10 Opening/closing something
P	11-12 Perceiving/examining/tinkering with something

P	1 A brief warning before it goes off
P	2-4 A tiny detail, easy to miss
P	5-7 Unusual construction/decor
P	8-10 Bait
P	11-12 Clear signs—it's obviously a trap
P	1d12 elements
HR
P	1 Camouflage/illusion/deception
P	2 Gravity/weight/mass/hardness
P	3 Blades/spikes/needles/pointy bits
P	4 Wire/rope/pulleys/contraptions
P	5 Tension/pressure/springs/balance
P	6 Chemics/poison/acid/gas/fire
P	7 Special materials (see below)
P	8 Runes/glyphs/sigils/marks/spells
P	9 Light/dark/heat/cold/noise/quiet
P	10 Thoughts/emotions/mind games
P	11 Spirits/constructs/undead/vermin
P	12 Previously triggered/disarmed Special materials might include <b>hazardous growths</b> (page 219), <b>orichalcum</b> (page 162), <b>black iron</b> (page 307), <b>dark ice</b> (page 322), <b>makerglass</b> (page 388), <b>aetherium</b> (page 404), <b>red crystal</b> (page 424), and/or other things of your devising.
P	<b>Examples:</b>
B	A pit, 15-feet deep, the bottom lined with rusty spikes; covered by taut fabric, pebbles, and dust
B	A gap runs down the ceiling of a low tunnel; stepping on a flagstone releases a swinging axe
B	A puzzle-box on a decoy coffin; futzing with it releases stabby little constructs from the coffin
B	A corpse's sword; moving it pulls a wire, which upends an urn full of salt and releases a trapped wraith
B	A rune-etched doorway; any who try to enter stop, turn around, and forget the last few minutes
B	Opening the door to the final vault
P	requires removing a keystone; the whole barrow will collapse
B	Sconces of glowing makerglass; break the rune-seal on the sarcophagus, get fried by lightning
B	A dead-end, the word VIGILANCE carved on the far wall, the room full of colorless, odorless gas; causes headaches, irritability, fainting, death

P	As you might expect, grave robbing was always a problem for the Barrow Builders.
P	But a clever sorcerer had a solution! So many hateful spirits roamed the world in those days. Why not bind some to the corpses of the deceased, and let the dead guard their own treasure?

P	• Flank and harry their foes
P	For a time, it was common for warriors to pledge both their lives and their deaths to their lieges, and to be interred with their horses and their fellows in their master's tomb. Thus, they could live on in death, still basking in a grim and joyless glory.

H3	Deathless ones
P	In the time of the Barrow Builders, many warlords and sorcerers were obsessed with immortality. A number of them found it—or something like it—through undeath.
P	To create a deathless one, imagine a warlord (someone similar to a <b>Manmarcher</b> <b>chief</b>, page 289), a <b>sorcerer</b> (page 435), a <b>necromancer</b> (page 84), or a <b>hdour</b> (page 234). Consider making them <b>corrupted</b> (page 432) by the Things Below. Add the <i>undead</i> tag, and give them +4 HP because they are animated by more than biology.
P	From there, pick or roll for the tether that sustains them, how it sustains them, and its limitation. Then pick or roll for the deathless one's current state. Consider where and how they (or their influence) might be encountered. Let this all inform their story, their personality, and their stat block.
P	1d12 tether
HR
P	1-2 Small (needle, torc, ring, etc.)
P	3-4 ◇ (sword, scepter, crown, scroll, mummified hand, etc.)
P	5-6 ◇◇ (shield, standard, urn, etc.)
P	7-8 ◇◇, <i>cumbersome</i> (bust, cauldron, coffer, tapestry, etc.)
P	9-10 <i>immobile</i> (hoard, tree, cave, statue, sarcophagus, etc.)
P	11-12 <i>fragile</i> and roll d10 again (egg, porcelain, mirror, device, etc.)
P	1d12 how it sustains them
HR
P	1-2 It hides their death/heart/soul
P	3-4 It anchors their soul to the world
P	5-6 It feeds/renews/recharges them
P	7-8 It gives them leverage over the <b>Lady of Crows</b> (page 71)
P	9-10 It shields them from the Lady and the <b>Pale Hunter</b> (page 292)
